narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked near the middle of their class. This low standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor by pulling the prediction toward passing. At 36, your score sits only slightly below the 37.18 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance about your abilities.

Your undergraduate GPA came third. At 3.40 it actually exceeded the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, so this feature also nudged the outcome toward success, though not enough to overcome the effect of your third-year ranking.

Taken together, the model saw your notably weak class standing in year three as the dominant signal, outweighing the positive contributions from your LSAT and college grades. 

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in later law school years or consider retaking the LSAT to strengthen that score before reapplying.
